Reference: Arkhangelsky et al. (2021)

Model Setting

The paper proposes synthetic difference in differences (SDID), an estimator of causal effects in panel data that combines the two dominant tools of applied work. Difference in differences (DID) is used when many units are treated and the researcher accepts parallel trends, so that additive unit and time fixed effects control for selection. Synthetic control (SC) is used when one or a few units are treated, and it reweights control units so that their pre-treatment path matches that of the treated units. The paper argues that the assumptions behind the two methods are closely related. Like SC, SDID reweights and matches pre-exposure trends, which weakens the reliance on parallel trends. Like DID, it is invariant to additive unit-level shifts and allows valid large-panel inference. It adds time weights, which put more weight on pre-treatment periods that resemble the post-treatment periods.

The paper has four parts. An application to California's Proposition 99 shows how the three estimators differ. Placebo simulations calibrated to the Current Population Survey and the Penn World Table show that SDID has lower bias and root-mean-squared error than DID, SC and two other benchmarks in almost all designs. The formal results show that, under a latent factor model for the systematic part of outcomes, SDID is consistent and asymptotically normal under conditions weaker than those needed for DID, for SC or for methods that estimate the factor structure. Finally, three variance estimators (bootstrap, jackknife and placebo) give confidence intervals with coverage close to nominal.

Setup and the Three Estimators

Consider a balanced panel with NNN units and TTT periods, outcome YitY_{it}Yit​ and binary treatment Wit∈{0,1}W_{it}\in\{0,1\}Wit​∈{0,1}. The first NcoN_{co}Nco​ units (controls) are never treated, and the last Ntr=N−NcoN_{tr}=N-N_{co}Ntr​=N−Nco​ units (treated) are exposed after period TpreT_{pre}Tpre​, so that there are Tpost=T−TpreT_{post}=T-T_{pre}Tpost​=T−Tpre​ post-treatment periods. This is block treatment assignment, Wit=1({i>Nco,t>Tpre})W_{it}=\mathbf{1}(\{i>N_{co},t>T_{pre}\})Wit​=1({i>Nco​,t>Tpre​}). Given unit weights ω^isdid\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_iω^isdid​ and time weights λ^tsdid\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}_tλ^tsdid​, the SDID estimator of the average effect τ\tauτ is a weighted two-way fixed effects regression:

(τ^sdid,μ^,α^,β^)=arg⁡min⁡τ,μ,α,β{∑i=1N∑t=1T(Yit−μ−αi−βt−Witτ)2ω^isdidλ^tsdid}(1)\left(\hat{\tau}^{sdid},\hat{\mu},\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}\right)=\arg\min_{\tau,\mu,\alpha,\beta}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(Y_{it}-\mu-\alpha_i-\beta_t-W_{it}\tau\right)^2\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_i\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}_t\right\} \tag{1}(τ^sdid,μ^​,α^,β^​)=argτ,μ,α,βmin​{i=1∑N​t=1∑T​(Yit​−μ−αi​−βt​−Wit​τ)2ω^isdid​λ^tsdid​}(1)

DID solves the same problem without unit or time weights:

(τ^did,μ^,α^,β^)=arg⁡min⁡α,β,μ,τ{∑i=1N∑t=1T(Yit−μ−αi−βt−Witτ)2}(2)\left(\hat{\tau}^{did},\hat{\mu},\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}\right)=\arg\min_{\alpha,\beta,\mu,\tau}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(Y_{it}-\mu-\alpha_i-\beta_t-W_{it}\tau\right)^2\right\} \tag{2}(τ^did,μ^​,α^,β^​)=argα,β,μ,τmin​{i=1∑N​t=1∑T​(Yit​−μ−αi​−βt​−Wit​τ)2}(2)

and SC omits the unit fixed effects and the time weights:

(τ^sc,μ^,β^)=arg⁡min⁡μ,β,τ{∑i=1N∑t=1T(Yit−μ−βt−Witτ)2ω^isc}(3)\left(\hat{\tau}^{sc},\hat{\mu},\hat{\beta}\right)=\arg\min_{\mu,\beta,\tau}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(Y_{it}-\mu-\beta_t-W_{it}\tau\right)^2\hat{\omega}^{sc}_i\right\} \tag{3}(τ^sc,μ^​,β^​)=argμ,β,τmin​{i=1∑N​t=1∑T​(Yit​−μ−βt​−Wit​τ)2ω^isc​}(3)

where μ\muμ is an intercept, αi\alpha_iαi​ are unit fixed effects and βt\beta_tβt​ are time fixed effects. The weights make the regression local: it emphasizes control units whose past resembles that of the treated units, and pre-treatment periods that resemble the treated periods. This makes the estimator more robust, and it can also improve precision by removing predictable parts of the outcome. The precision gain is not guaranteed: with little systematic heterogeneity across units or periods, unequal weights can make SDID less precise than DID. The unit fixed effects make the model more flexible and often explain much of the variation in outcomes. SC weights can replace them only if the weighted average of control outcomes equals the treated average exactly in the pre-treatment periods, which in practice holds only approximately. The same benefit is obtained by applying SC after subtracting each unit's pre-treatment mean, the estimator of Doudchenko and Imbens (2016) and Ferman and Pinto (2019), called DIFP. It is reported throughout to separate the role of fixed effects from the role of time weights.

Unit and Time Weights

The unit weights are chosen so that the weighted average of control outcomes is parallel to the average treated outcome before treatment, ∑i=1Ncoω^isdidYit≈Ntr−1∑i=Nco+1NYit\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_iY_{it}\approx N_{tr}^{-1}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}Y_{it}∑i=1Nco​​ω^isdid​Yit​≈Ntr−1​∑i=Nco​+1N​Yit​ for all t=1,…,Tpret=1,\dots,T_{pre}t=1,…,Tpre​. They solve (ω^0,ω^sdid)=arg⁡min⁡ω0∈R,ω∈Ωℓunit(ω0,ω)(\hat{\omega}_0,\hat{\omega}^{sdid})=\arg\min_{\omega_0\in\mathbb{R},\omega\in\Omega}\ell_{unit}(\omega_0,\omega)(ω^0​,ω^sdid)=argminω0​∈R,ω∈Ω​ℓunit​(ω0​,ω) with:

ℓunit(ω0,ω)=∑t=1Tpre(ω0+∑i=1NcoωiYit−1Ntr∑i=Nco+1NYit)2+ζ2Tpre∥ω∥22Ω={ω∈R+N:∑i=1Ncoωi=1, ωi=Ntr−1 for all i=Nco+1,…,N}(4)\begin{aligned} \ell_{unit}\left(\omega_0,\omega\right)&=\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\left(\omega_0+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\omega_iY_{it}-\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}Y_{it}\right)^2+\zeta^2T_{pre}\lVert\omega\rVert_2^2\\ \Omega&=\left\{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^N_+:\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\omega_i=1,\ \omega_i=N_{tr}^{-1}\text{ for all }i=N_{co}+1,\dots,N\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{4}ℓunit​(ω0​,ω)Ω​=t=1∑Tpre​​(ω0​+i=1∑Nco​​ωi​Yit​−Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​Yit​)2+ζ2Tpre​∥ω∥22​={ω∈R+N​:i=1∑Nco​​ωi​=1, ωi​=Ntr−1​ for all i=Nco​+1,…,N}​(4)

where R+\mathbb{R}_+R+​ is the positive real line. The regularization parameter ζ\zetaζ is set to:

ζ=(NtrTpost)1/4σ^,σ^2=1Nco(Tpre−1)∑i=1Nco∑t=1Tpre−1(Δit−Δˉ)2(5)\zeta=\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{1/4}\hat{\sigma},\qquad\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{N_{co}\left(T_{pre}-1\right)}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}-1}\left(\Delta_{it}-\bar{\Delta}\right)^2 \tag{5}ζ=(Ntr​Tpost​)1/4σ^,σ^2=Nco​(Tpre​−1)1​i=1∑Nco​​t=1∑Tpre​−1​(Δit​−Δˉ)2(5)

with:

Δit=Yi(t+1)−Yit,Δˉ=1Nco(Tpre−1)∑i=1Nco∑t=1Tpre−1Δit(6)\Delta_{it}=Y_{i(t+1)}-Y_{it},\qquad\bar{\Delta}=\frac{1}{N_{co}\left(T_{pre}-1\right)}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}-1}\Delta_{it} \tag{6}Δit​=Yi(t+1)​−Yit​,Δˉ=Nco​(Tpre​−1)1​i=1∑Nco​​t=1∑Tpre​−1​Δit​(6)

so that ζ\zetaζ equals the size of a typical one-period change in the outcome of control units before treatment, times a theoretically motivated factor (NtrTpost)1/4(N_{tr}T_{post})^{1/4}(Ntr​Tpost​)1/4. These weights differ from those of Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) in two ways. First, the intercept ω0\omega_0ω0​ means that the weighted controls need not match the level of the treated pre-trend, only be parallel to it. This is allowed because the fixed effects αi\alpha_iαi​ absorb constant differences between units. Second, the ridge penalty raises the dispersion of the weights and makes them unique. Without ω0\omega_0ω0​ and with ζ=0\zeta=0ζ=0 the problem is exactly the original SC problem for Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1.

The time weights balance pre-treatment and post-treatment periods for the control units. They solve (λ^0,λ^sdid)=arg⁡min⁡λ0∈R,λ∈Λℓtime(λ0,λ)(\hat{\lambda}_0,\hat{\lambda}^{sdid})=\arg\min_{\lambda_0\in\mathbb{R},\lambda\in\Lambda}\ell_{time}(\lambda_0,\lambda)(λ^0​,λ^sdid)=argminλ0​∈R,λ∈Λ​ℓtime​(λ0​,λ) with:

ℓtime(λ0,λ)=∑i=1Nco(λ0+∑t=1TpreλtYit−1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1TYit)2Λ={λ∈R+T:∑t=1Tpreλt=1, λt=Tpost−1 for all t=Tpre+1,…,T}(7)\begin{aligned} \ell_{time}\left(\lambda_0,\lambda\right)&=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\left(\lambda_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\lambda_tY_{it}-\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}Y_{it}\right)^2\\ \Lambda&=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^T_+:\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\lambda_t=1,\ \lambda_t=T_{post}^{-1}\text{ for all }t=T_{pre}+1,\dots,T\right\} \end{aligned} \tag{7}ℓtime​(λ0​,λ)Λ​=i=1∑Nco​​​λ0​+t=1∑Tpre​​λt​Yit​−Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​Yit​​2=⎩⎨⎧​λ∈R+T​:t=1∑Tpre​​λt​=1, λt​=Tpost−1​ for all t=Tpre​+1,…,T⎭⎬⎫​​(7)

The time problem is not regularized. The reason is that the theory allows errors to be correlated over time within a unit but not across units within a period, beyond what the factor structure captures. Because ℓtime\ell_{time}ℓtime​ can have several minima, the implementation adds a very small penalty ζ2Nco∥λ∥2\zeta^2N_{co}\lVert\lambda\rVert^2ζ2Nco​∥λ∥2 with ζ=10−6σ^\zeta=10^{-6}\hat{\sigma}ζ=10−6σ^. The SC and DIFP estimators reported in the paper use unit weights from the same problem with this minimal regularization, and SC also drops ω0\omega_0ω0​. The procedure (Algorithm 1) is: compute ζ\zetaζ, compute ω^sdid\hat{\omega}^{sdid}ω^sdid, compute λ^sdid\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}λ^sdid, run the weighted regression. Time-varying exogenous covariates Xit∈RpX_{it}\in\mathbb{R}^pXit​∈Rp are handled by applying SDID to the residuals Yitres=Yit−Xitβ^Y^{res}_{it}=Y_{it}-X_{it}\hat{\beta}Yitres​=Yit​−Xit​β^​ of a regression of YitY_{it}Yit​ on XitX_{it}Xit​.

All three estimators can be written as a weighted difference in adjusted outcomes δ^i\hat{\delta}_iδ^i​:

τ^=δ^tr−∑i=1Ncoω^iδ^i,δ^tr=1Ntr∑i=Nco+1Nδ^i(8)\hat{\tau}=\hat{\delta}_{tr}-\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\hat{\omega}_i\hat{\delta}_i,\qquad\hat{\delta}_{tr}=\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}\hat{\delta}_i \tag{8}τ^=δ^tr​−i=1∑Nco​​ω^i​δ^i​,δ^tr​=Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​δ^i​(8)

where DID uses ω^idid=Nco−1\hat{\omega}^{did}_i=N_{co}^{-1}ω^idid​=Nco−1​ and the adjusted outcomes are:

δ^isc=1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1TYitδ^idid=1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1TYit−1Tpre∑t=1TpreYitδ^isdid=1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1TYit−∑t=1Tpreλ^tsdidYit(9)\begin{aligned} \hat{\delta}^{sc}_i&=\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}Y_{it}\\ \hat{\delta}^{did}_i&=\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}Y_{it}-\frac{1}{T_{pre}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}Y_{it}\\ \hat{\delta}^{sdid}_i&=\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}Y_{it}-\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}_tY_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{9}δ^isc​δ^idid​δ^isdid​​=Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​Yit​=Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​Yit​−Tpre​1​t=1∑Tpre​​Yit​=Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​Yit​−t=1∑Tpre​​λ^tsdid​Yit​​(9)

SC compares post-treatment averages, DID compares the change from the unweighted pre-treatment average, and SDID compares the change from a weighted pre-treatment average. DID gives every pre-treatment period the same weight, and event studies implicitly put all the weight on the last pre-treatment period. SDID chooses the periods from the data.

Application: California Proposition 99

The application revisits Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010). The data cover per capita cigarette sales (packs per year) in 39 states from 1970 to 2000. California raised cigarette taxes from 1989, so Tpre=19T_{pre}=19Tpre​=19, Tpost=12T_{post}=12Tpost​=12, Nco=38N_{co}=38Nco​=38 and Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1. Standard errors come from the placebo method described below.

  • Point estimates: the average effect over the 12 post-treatment years is −15.6-15.6−15.6 (8.4) for SDID, −19.6-19.6−19.6 (9.9) for SC and −27.3-27.3−27.3 (17.7) for DID. The matrix completion (MC) estimator of Athey et al. (2021) gives −20.2-20.2−20.2 (11.5) and DIFP gives −11.1-11.1−11.1 (9.5).

  • Interpretation: pre-treatment trends are visibly not parallel, so the DID estimate is suspect and likely overstates the effect. The gap between SDID and SC shows that time weights and unit fixed effects change the conclusion. The standard errors of SDID, SC, DIFP and MC are smaller than that of DID even though these methods are more flexible, because weighting improves the local fit.

  • Weights: SC unit weights are sparse. SDID unit weights are also sparse but less so, because of the regularization and the intercept ω0\omega_0ω0​. In the figure the SDID time weights are concentrated on a few years just before 1989. DID and SC each have states with very high influence, measured by ω^i(δ^tr−δ^i)\hat{\omega}_i(\hat{\delta}_{tr}-\hat{\delta}_i)ω^i​(δ^tr​−δ^i​) (New Hampshire in both cases), and SDID has none.

Latent Factor Model and Placebo Designs

The simulations are built on a latent factor model (interactive fixed effects), Yit=γiυt⊤+τWit+εitY_{it}=\gamma_i\upsilon_t^{\top}+\tau W_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}Yit​=γi​υt⊤​+τWit​+εit​ with unit factors γi\gamma_iγi​ and time factors υt\upsilon_tυt​ of dimension RRR, or in matrix form:

Y=L+τW+E,L=ΓΥ⊤(10)\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{L}+\tau\mathbf{W}+\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{\Gamma}\mathbf{\Upsilon}^{\top} \tag{10}Y=L+τW+E,L=ΓΥ⊤(10)

where L\mathbf{L}L is the systematic component and E\mathbf{E}E the error matrix. The conditional expectation of E\mathbf{E}E given W\mathbf{W}W and L\mathbf{L}L is zero, so assignment cannot depend on E\mathbf{E}E. Assignment may depend on L\mathbf{L}L, so W\mathbf{W}W is not randomized. Rows Ei\mathbf{E}_iEi​ are independent across units and may be correlated over time. If Lit=αi+βtL_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_tLit​=αi​+βt​, DID is consistent for τ\tauτ, and interactions in L\mathbf{L}L are what make DID misspecified.

The first study follows Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004) and uses log wages of women with positive wages in the CPS, averaged by state and year for 1979 to 2019. The rows of the error matrix are drawn as Ei∼N(0,Σ)\mathbf{E}_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)Ei​∼N(0,Σ). The systematic component L\mathbf{L}L is the best rank-four approximation to the matrix of actual state-year averages Yit∗Y^*_{it}Yit∗​, and Σ\SigmaΣ comes from an AR(2) model fitted to the residuals Yit∗−LitY^*_{it}-L_{it}Yit∗​−Lit​. The systematic component is split into an additive part F\mathbf{F}F and an interactive part M\mathbf{M}M:

Fit=αi+βt=1T∑l=1TLil+1N∑j=1NLjt−1NT∑itLit,Mit=Lit−Fit(11)F_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_t=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{l=1}^{T}L_{il}+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}L_{jt}-\frac{1}{NT}\sum_{it}L_{it},\qquad M_{it}=L_{it}-F_{it} \tag{11}Fit​=αi​+βt​=T1​l=1∑T​Lil​+N1​j=1∑N​Ljt​−NT1​it∑​Lit​,Mit​=Lit​−Fit​(11)

The true effect is zero. Treatment is Wit=Di1t>T0W_{it}=D_i\mathbf{1}_{t>T_0}Wit​=Di​1t>T0​​, and the exposure indicator DiD_iDi​ is correlated with the systematic component:

Di∣Ei,αi,Mi∼Bernoulli(πi),πi=π(αi,Mi;ϕ)=exp⁡(ϕααi+ϕMMi)1+exp⁡(ϕααi+ϕMMi)(12)D_i\mid\mathbf{E}_i,\alpha_i,\mathbf{M}_i\sim\text{Bernoulli}\left(\pi_i\right),\qquad\pi_i=\pi\left(\alpha_i,\mathbf{M}_i;\phi\right)=\frac{\exp\left(\phi_{\alpha}\alpha_i+\phi_M\mathbf{M}_i\right)}{1+\exp\left(\phi_{\alpha}\alpha_i+\phi_M\mathbf{M}_i\right)} \tag{12}Di​∣Ei​,αi​,Mi​∼Bernoulli(πi​),πi​=π(αi​,Mi​;ϕ)=1+exp(ϕα​αi​+ϕM​Mi​)exp(ϕα​αi​+ϕM​Mi​)​(12)

The coefficients ϕ\phiϕ are estimated by a logistic regression of an observed state characteristic on Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​ and αi\alpha_iαi​. Three characteristics are used (minimum wage laws, abortion rights, gun control laws), and the fit has an R2R^2R2 of 15 to 30 percent. Assignment is strictly exogenous, since DiD_iDi​ is independent of Ei\mathbf{E}_iEi​. With completely random assignment the presence of L\mathbf{L}L creates no bias for any method. With this non-uniform assignment, methods that ignore L\mathbf{L}L are biased. The panel has N=50N=50N=50 and T=40T=40T=40, outcomes are normalized to mean zero and unit variance, and the baseline has Tpost=10T_{post}=10Tpost​=10 and at most Ntr=10N_{tr}=10Ntr​=10. The component sizes in the baseline are ∥F∥F/NT=0.992\lVert\mathbf{F}\rVert_F/\sqrt{NT}=0.992∥F∥F​/NT​=0.992, ∥M∥F/NT=0.100\lVert\mathbf{M}\rVert_F/\sqrt{NT}=0.100∥M∥F​/NT​=0.100 and tr(Σ)/T=0.098\sqrt{\text{tr}(\Sigma)/T}=0.098tr(Σ)/T​=0.098, and the AR(2) coefficients are (ρ−1,ρ−2)=(0.01,−0.06)(\rho_{-1},\rho_{-2})=(0.01,-0.06)(ρ−1​,ρ−2​)=(0.01,−0.06). The designs vary the outcome model (dropping F\mathbf{F}F, M\mathbf{M}M, the noise or its serial correlation), the assignment process, the outcome variable (hours, unemployment rate) and the size of the treated block.

The second study uses log real GDP from the Penn World Table for N=111N=111N=111 countries and T=48T=48T=48 years starting in 1959, a setting closer to SC applications. It is built in the same way, with Ntr=10N_{tr}=10Ntr​=10 and Tpost=10T_{post}=10Tpost​=10. Assignment is based on democracy indicators, on education indicators, or is completely random. Two-way fixed effects again explain most of the variation, but the interactive component is larger than in the CPS.

Placebo Results

All figures are multiplied by ten, as in the paper's tables, and are based on 1,000 replications.

  • CPS baseline: the RMSE is 0.28 for SDID, 0.37 for SC, 0.49 for DID, 0.35 for MC and 0.32 for DIFP. The bias is 0.10, 0.20, 0.21, 0.15 and 0.07.

  • Dropping components: without M\mathbf{M}M the fixed effects model is correct and DID and MC are best (0.14, against 0.16 for SDID and 0.18 for SC). Without F\mathbf{F}F SC is best (0.23, against 0.28 for SDID and 0.49 for DID). With only noise all estimators are close (0.14 to 0.16). Without noise SDID (0.06) and MC (0.04) are far ahead of SC (0.17) and DID (0.47).

  • Assignment: under random assignment all methods are nearly unbiased, and SDID is more precise (0.24, against 0.44 for DID). The reason is that it exploits predictable variation by matching on pre-exposure trends.

  • Other outcomes and block sizes: for the unemployment rate the RMSE is 2.25 (SDID), 2.31 (SC) and 3.91 (DID), and every method has a large bias (1.77, 1.73 and 3.60). With Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1 it is 0.63, 0.73 and 1.26. For average hours MC (1.85) is slightly ahead of SDID (1.90).

  • Penn World Table: the RMSE of SDID, SC and DID is 0.31, 0.38 and 1.97 under democracy assignment, 0.30, 0.53 and 1.72 under education assignment, and 0.37, 0.46 and 1.29 under random assignment. The bias of DID is 1.75 and 1.62 in the first two designs, against −0.05-0.05−0.05 and −0.03-0.03−0.03 for SDID. DID does much worse relative to SC than in the CPS, because the interactive component is stronger.

Formal Setting and Weighted Double Differencing

The formal results allow heterogeneous effects. The model and the estimand, the average effect on the treated cells, are:

Y=L+W∘τ+E,(W∘τ)it=Witτit,τ=1NtrTpost∑i=Nco+1N∑t=Tpre+1Tτit(13)\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{L}+\mathbf{W}\circ\boldsymbol{\tau}+\mathbf{E},\qquad\left(\mathbf{W}\circ\boldsymbol{\tau}\right)_{it}=W_{it}\tau_{it},\qquad\tau=\frac{1}{N_{tr}T_{post}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}\tau_{it} \tag{13}Y=L+W∘τ+E,(W∘τ)it​=Wit​τit​,τ=Ntr​Tpost​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​t=Tpre​+1∑T​τit​(13)

The factors are defined from the singular value decomposition L=UDV⊤\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^{\top}L=UDV⊤ as Γ=UD1/2\mathbf{\Gamma}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}^{1/2}Γ=UD1/2 and Υ⊤=D1/2V⊤\mathbf{\Upsilon}^{\top}=\mathbf{D}^{1/2}\mathbf{V}^{\top}Υ⊤=D1/2V⊤. Each matrix is partitioned into four blocks, such as Yco,pre\mathbf{Y}_{co,pre}Yco,pre​, Yco,post\mathbf{Y}_{co,post}Yco,post​, Ytr,pre\mathbf{Y}_{tr,pre}Ytr,pre​ and Ytr,post\mathbf{Y}_{tr,post}Ytr,post​. Errors are homoskedastic across units but not across time, var[Ei⋅]=Σ∈RT×T\text{var}[\mathbf{E}_{i\cdot}]=\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}var[Ei⋅​]=Σ∈RT×T, with blocks Σpre,pre\Sigma_{pre,pre}Σpre,pre​, Σpre,post\Sigma_{pre,post}Σpre,post​, Σpost,pre\Sigma_{post,pre}Σpost,pre​ and Σpost,post\Sigma_{post,post}Σpost,post​. For any ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omegaω∈Ω and λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambdaλ∈Λ define the weighted double-differencing estimator:

τ^(ω,λ)=ωtr⊤Ytr,postλpost−ωco⊤Yco,postλpost−ωtr⊤Ytr,preλpre+ωco⊤Yco,preλpre(14)\hat{\tau}\left(\omega,\lambda\right)=\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}_{tr,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}_{co,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}_{tr,pre}\lambda_{pre}+\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}_{co,pre}\lambda_{pre} \tag{14}τ^(ω,λ)=ωtr⊤​Ytr,post​λpost​−ωco⊤​Yco,post​λpost​−ωtr⊤​Ytr,pre​λpre​+ωco⊤​Yco,pre​λpre​(14)

DID has this form with constant weights, and SDID has it with ω^sdid\hat{\omega}^{sdid}ω^sdid and λ^sdid\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}λ^sdid, written ω^\hat{\omega}ω^ and λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^ below. Since ωtr\omega_{tr}ωtr​ and λpost\lambda_{post}λpost​ have all elements equal to 1/Ntr1/N_{tr}1/Ntr​ and 1/Tpost1/T_{post}1/Tpost​, ωtr⊤τtr,postλpost=τ\omega_{tr}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{tr,post}\lambda_{post}=\tauωtr⊤​τtr,post​λpost​=τ, and the error splits into a bias and a noise term:

τ^(ω,λ)−τ=B(ω,λ)+ε(ω,λ)B(ω,λ)=ωtr⊤Ltr,postλpost−ωco⊤Lco,postλpost−ωtr⊤Ltr,preλpre+ωco⊤Lco,preλpreε(ω,λ)=ωtr⊤Etr,postλpost−ωco⊤Eco,postλpost−ωtr⊤Etr,preλpre+ωco⊤Eco,preλpre(15)\begin{aligned} \hat{\tau}\left(\omega,\lambda\right)-\tau&=B\left(\omega,\lambda\right)+\varepsilon\left(\omega,\lambda\right)\\ B\left(\omega,\lambda\right)&=\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\lambda_{pre}+\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\lambda_{pre}\\ \varepsilon\left(\omega,\lambda\right)&=\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{tr,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{co,post}\lambda_{post}-\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{tr,pre}\lambda_{pre}+\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{E}_{co,pre}\lambda_{pre} \end{aligned} \tag{15}τ^(ω,λ)−τB(ω,λ)ε(ω,λ)​=B(ω,λ)+ε(ω,λ)=ωtr⊤​Ltr,post​λpost​−ωco⊤​Lco,post​λpost​−ωtr⊤​Ltr,pre​λpre​+ωco⊤​Lco,pre​λpre​=ωtr⊤​Etr,post​λpost​−ωco⊤​Eco,post​λpost​−ωtr⊤​Etr,pre​λpre​+ωco⊤​Eco,pre​λpre​​(15)

SC removes the bias from L\mathbf{L}L only through unit weights that balance Γ\mathbf{\Gamma}Γ. SDID also uses time weights that balance Υ\mathbf{\Upsilon}Υ. In addition, the fixed effects and the intercepts ω0\omega_0ω0​ and λ0\lambda_0λ0​ make τ^sdid\hat{\tau}^{sdid}τ^sdid invariant to replacing LitL_{it}Lit​ by Lit+αi+βtL_{it}+\alpha_i+\beta_tLit​+αi​+βt​. DID shares this invariance. SC is invariant only to shifts in βt\beta_tβt​.

Oracle Weights and Error Decomposition

The weights ω^\hat{\omega}ω^ and λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^ are data dependent. To handle this the paper defines deterministic oracle weights that minimize the expected objectives:

(ω~0,ω~)=arg⁡min⁡ω0∈R,ω∈ΩE[ℓunit(ω0,ω)],(λ~0,λ~)=arg⁡min⁡λ0∈R,λ∈ΛE[ℓtime(λ0,λ)](16)\left(\tilde{\omega}_0,\tilde{\omega}\right)=\arg\min_{\omega_0\in\mathbb{R},\omega\in\Omega}E\left[\ell_{unit}\left(\omega_0,\omega\right)\right],\qquad\left(\tilde{\lambda}_0,\tilde{\lambda}\right)=\arg\min_{\lambda_0\in\mathbb{R},\lambda\in\Lambda}E\left[\ell_{time}\left(\lambda_0,\lambda\right)\right] \tag{16}(ω~0​,ω~)=argω0​∈R,ω∈Ωmin​E[ℓunit​(ω0​,ω)],(λ~0​,λ~)=argλ0​∈R,λ∈Λmin​E[ℓtime​(λ0​,λ)](16)

Under the model these have a simple form. For the unit weights:

(ω~0,ω~)=arg⁡min⁡ω0∈R,ω∈Ω∥ω0+ωco⊤Lco,pre−ωtr⊤Ltr,pre∥22+(tr(Σpre,pre)+ζ2Tpre)∥ω∥22(17)\left(\tilde{\omega}_0,\tilde{\omega}\right)=\arg\min_{\omega_0\in\mathbb{R},\omega\in\Omega}\lVert\omega_0+\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}-\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\rVert_2^2+\left(\text{tr}\left(\Sigma_{pre,pre}\right)+\zeta^2T_{pre}\right)\lVert\omega\rVert_2^2 \tag{17}(ω~0​,ω~)=argω0​∈R,ω∈Ωmin​∥ω0​+ωco⊤​Lco,pre​−ωtr⊤​Ltr,pre​∥22​+(tr(Σpre,pre​)+ζ2Tpre​)∥ω∥22​(17)

and for the time weights:

(λ~0,λ~)=arg⁡min⁡λ0∈R,λ∈Λ∥λ0+Lco,preλpre−Lco,postλpost∥22+∥Σ~λ∥22,Σ~=(Σpre,pre−Σpre,post−Σpost,preΣpost,post)(18)\left(\tilde{\lambda}_0,\tilde{\lambda}\right)=\arg\min_{\lambda_0\in\mathbb{R},\lambda\in\Lambda}\lVert\lambda_0+\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\lambda_{pre}-\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\lambda_{post}\rVert_2^2+\lVert\tilde{\Sigma}\lambda\rVert_2^2,\qquad\tilde{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{pre,pre}&-\Sigma_{pre,post}\\-\Sigma_{post,pre}&\Sigma_{post,post}\end{pmatrix} \tag{18}(λ~0​,λ~)=argλ0​∈R,λ∈Λmin​∥λ0​+Lco,pre​λpre​−Lco,post​λpost​∥22​+∥Σ~λ∥22​,Σ~=(Σpre,pre​−Σpost,pre​​−Σpre,post​Σpost,post​​)(18)

The noise thus acts as an additional ridge penalty in both problems. The error of SDID is decomposed into three terms:

τ^sdid−τ=ε(ω~,λ~)⏟oracle noise+B(ω~,λ~)⏟oracle confounding bias+τ^(ω^,λ^)−τ^(ω~,λ~)⏟deviation from oracle(19)\hat{\tau}^{sdid}-\tau=\underbrace{\varepsilon\left(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda}\right)}_{\text{oracle noise}}+\underbrace{B\left(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda}\right)}_{\text{oracle confounding bias}}+\underbrace{\hat{\tau}\left(\hat{\omega},\hat{\lambda}\right)-\hat{\tau}\left(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda}\right)}_{\text{deviation from oracle}} \tag{19}τ^sdid−τ=oracle noiseε(ω~,λ~)​​+oracle confounding biasB(ω~,λ~)​​+deviation from oracleτ^(ω^,λ^)−τ^(ω~,λ~)​​(19)

The oracle noise is small when the weights are not too concentrated and there are enough treated units and periods. With Σ=σ2IT×T\Sigma=\sigma^2I_{T\times T}Σ=σ2IT×T​ its variance is var[ε(ω~,λ~)]=σ2(Ntr−1+∥ω~∥22)(Tpost−1+∥λ~∥22)\text{var}[\varepsilon(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda})]=\sigma^2(N_{tr}^{-1}+\lVert\tilde{\omega}\rVert_2^2)(T_{post}^{-1}+\lVert\tilde{\lambda}\rVert_2^2)var[ε(ω~,λ~)]=σ2(Ntr−1​+∥ω~∥22​)(Tpost−1​+∥λ~∥22​). The asymptotic analysis makes this term dominant. The oracle confounding bias can be written in two ways:

B(ω,λ)=(ωtr⊤Ltr,post−ωco⊤Lco,post)λpost−(ωtr⊤Ltr,pre−ωco⊤Lco,pre)λpre=ωtr⊤(Ltr,postλpost−Ltr,preλpre)−ωco⊤(Lco,postλpost−Lco,preλpre)(20)\begin{aligned} B\left(\omega,\lambda\right)&=\left(\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}-\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\right)\lambda_{post}-\left(\omega_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}-\omega_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\right)\lambda_{pre}\\ &=\omega_{tr}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}\lambda_{post}-\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\lambda_{pre}\right)-\omega_{co}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\lambda_{post}-\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\lambda_{pre}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{20}B(ω,λ)​=(ωtr⊤​Ltr,post​−ωco⊤​Lco,post​)λpost​−(ωtr⊤​Ltr,pre​−ωco⊤​Lco,pre​)λpre​=ωtr⊤​(Ltr,post​λpost​−Ltr,pre​λpre​)−ωco⊤​(Lco,post​λpost​−Lco,pre​λpre​)​(20)

This is the double robustness of SDID. The bias is small if the oracle row regression fits the pre-treatment columns and generalizes to the post-treatment columns, that is, ω~0+ω~co⊤Lco,pre≈ω~tr⊤Ltr,pre\tilde{\omega}_0+\tilde{\omega}_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\approx\tilde{\omega}_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}ω~0​+ω~co⊤​Lco,pre​≈ω~tr⊤​Ltr,pre​ and ω~0+ω~co⊤Lco,post≈ω~tr⊤Ltr,post\tilde{\omega}_0+\tilde{\omega}_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\approx\tilde{\omega}_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}ω~0​+ω~co⊤​Lco,post​≈ω~tr⊤​Ltr,post​. It is also small if the oracle column regression fits the control rows and generalizes to the treated rows, that is, λ~0+Lco,preλ~pre≈Lco,postλ~post\tilde{\lambda}_0+\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}\approx\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\tilde{\lambda}_{post}λ~0​+Lco,pre​λ~pre​≈Lco,post​λ~post​ and λ~0+Ltr,preλ~pre≈Ltr,postλ~post\tilde{\lambda}_0+\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}\approx\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}\tilde{\lambda}_{post}λ~0​+Ltr,pre​λ~pre​≈Ltr,post​λ~post​. Even if neither holds, it is enough that one model predicts the generalization error of the other. The property parallels augmented inverse probability weighting, where the outcome model and the assignment model can substitute for each other. That one of the regressions generalizes to the exposed rows or columns is an identification assumption without clear testable implications, an assumption of no unexplained confounding. The deviation from oracle is small when the oracle weights fit well on their own training sets and ∥ω~∥2\lVert\tilde{\omega}\rVert_2∥ω~∥2​ and ∥λ~∥2\lVert\tilde{\lambda}\rVert_2∥λ~∥2​ are not too large.

When Σ\SigmaΣ is not diagonal, the penalty in the time problem shrinks λ~pre\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}λ~pre​ not towards zero but towards an autoregression vector:

ψ=arg⁡min⁡v∈RTpre∥Σ~(vλpost)∥=Σpre,pre−1Σpre,postλpost(21)\psi=\arg\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{pre}}}\left\lVert\tilde{\Sigma}\begin{pmatrix}v\\\lambda_{post}\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert=\Sigma_{pre,pre}^{-1}\Sigma_{pre,post}\lambda_{post} \tag{21}ψ=argv∈RTpre​min​​Σ~(vλpost​​)​=Σpre,pre−1​Σpre,post​λpost​(21)

which is the population coefficient of a regression of the average post-treatment error on the pre-treatment errors. Without autocorrelation ψ\psiψ is zero. With autocorrelation, shrinking towards ψ\psiψ lowers the variance, so SDID can be more precise than DID even when the two-way fixed effects model is correct.

Assumptions

  • Assumption 1 (errors): the rows Ei\mathbf{E}_iEi​ are independent and identically distributed Gaussian vectors, and the eigenvalues of Σ\SigmaΣ are bounded and bounded away from zero.

  • Assumption 2 (sample sizes): NtrTpost→∞N_{tr}T_{post}\to\inftyNtr​Tpost​→∞ and both NcoN_{co}Nco​ and TpreT_{pre}Tpre​ go to infinity; Tpre/NcoT_{pre}/N_{co}Tpre​/Nco​ is bounded and bounded away from zero; and Nco/(NtrTpostmax⁡(Ntr,Tpost)log⁡2(Nco))→∞N_{co}/(N_{tr}T_{post}\max(N_{tr},T_{post})\log^2(N_{co}))\to\inftyNco​/(Ntr​Tpost​max(Ntr​,Tpost​)log2(Nco​))→∞. The panel is large and the treated block grows more slowly than the panel. One of TpostT_{post}Tpost​ and NtrN_{tr}Ntr​ may stay fixed, but not both.

  • Assumption 3 (properties of L\mathbf{L}L): with σ1,σ2,…\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\dotsσ1​,σ2​,… the singular values in decreasing order and RRR the largest integer less than min⁡(Tpre,Nco)\sqrt{\min(T_{pre},N_{co})}min(Tpre​,Nco​)​, the condition in the first equation below holds. A rank of L\mathbf{L}L below min⁡(Tpre,Nco)\sqrt{\min(T_{pre},N_{co})}min(Tpre​,Nco​)​ is sufficient. No lower bound on the non-zero singular values is needed.

  • Assumption 4 (weights and L\mathbf{L}L): the oracle weights are dispersed, fit well on their training blocks, and jointly remove the bias, as in the second and third equations below. This plays the role of the identifying assumption linking L\mathbf{L}L and W\mathbf{W}W.

The spectral condition is:

σR(Lco,pre)/R=o(min⁡{Ntr−1/2log⁡−1/2(Nco),Tpost−1/2log⁡−1/2(Tpre)})(22)\sigma_R\left(\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\right)/R=o\left(\min\left\{N_{tr}^{-1/2}\log^{-1/2}\left(N_{co}\right),T_{post}^{-1/2}\log^{-1/2}\left(T_{pre}\right)\right\}\right) \tag{22}σR​(Lco,pre​)/R=o(min{Ntr−1/2​log−1/2(Nco​),Tpost−1/2​log−1/2(Tpre​)})(22)

The conditions on the oracle unit weights (first two lines) and time weights (last two lines) are:

∥ω~co∥2=o([(NtrTpost)log⁡(Nco)]−1/2)∥ω~0+ω~co⊤Lco,pre−ω~tr⊤Ltr,pre∥2=o(Nco1/4(NtrTpostmax⁡(Nco,Tpost))−1/4log⁡−1/2(Nco))∥λ~pre−ψ∥2=o([(NtrTpost)log⁡(Nco)]−1/2)∥λ~0+Lco,preλ~pre−Lco,postλ~post∥2=o(Nco1/4(NtrTpost)−1/8)(23)\begin{aligned} \lVert\tilde{\omega}_{co}\rVert_2&=o\left(\left[\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)\log\left(N_{co}\right)\right]^{-1/2}\right)\\ \lVert\tilde{\omega}_0+\tilde{\omega}_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}-\tilde{\omega}_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\rVert_2&=o\left(N_{co}^{1/4}\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\max\left(N_{co},T_{post}\right)\right)^{-1/4}\log^{-1/2}\left(N_{co}\right)\right)\\ \lVert\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}-\psi\rVert_2&=o\left(\left[\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)\log\left(N_{co}\right)\right]^{-1/2}\right)\\ \lVert\tilde{\lambda}_0+\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}-\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\tilde{\lambda}_{post}\rVert_2&=o\left(N_{co}^{1/4}\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{-1/8}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{23}∥ω~co​∥2​∥ω~0​+ω~co⊤​Lco,pre​−ω~tr⊤​Ltr,pre​∥2​∥λ~pre​−ψ∥2​∥λ~0​+Lco,pre​λ~pre​−Lco,post​λ~post​∥2​​=o([(Ntr​Tpost​)log(Nco​)]−1/2)=o(Nco1/4​(Ntr​Tpost​max(Nco​,Tpost​))−1/4log−1/2(Nco​))=o([(Ntr​Tpost​)log(Nco​)]−1/2)=o(Nco1/4​(Ntr​Tpost​)−1/8)​(23)

and the joint condition is that the oracle bias is negligible:

ω~tr⊤Ltr,postλ~post−ω~co⊤Lco,postλ~post−ω~tr⊤Ltr,preλ~pre+ω~co⊤Lco,preλ~pre=o((NtrTpost)−1/2)(24)\tilde{\omega}_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}\tilde{\lambda}_{post}-\tilde{\omega}_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,post}\tilde{\lambda}_{post}-\tilde{\omega}_{tr}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}+\tilde{\omega}_{co}^{\top}\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}=o\left(\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \tag{24}ω~tr⊤​Ltr,post​λ~post​−ω~co⊤​Lco,post​λ~post​−ω~tr⊤​Ltr,pre​λ~pre​+ω~co⊤​Lco,pre​λ~pre​=o((Ntr​Tpost​)−1/2)(24)

These assumptions do not require that double differencing alone removes unit and time effects (the DID assumption), nor that unit comparisons alone remove the bias (the SC assumption), nor that a low-rank factor model is correctly specified (as in Bai 2009 and Moon and Weidner 2015, 2017). Only the combination of double differencing, unit weights and time weights must make the bias small. They hold in the well-specified two-way fixed effects model with uncorrelated homoskedastic errors, where the rank condition holds with R=2R=2R=2, the oracle unit weights on controls are 1/Nco1/N_{co}1/Nco​ and the oracle pre-treatment time weights are 1/Tpre1/T_{pre}1/Tpre​.

Theorem 1: Asymptotic Normality

Take L\mathbf{L}L and W\mathbf{W}W as fixed, let the regularization parameter satisfy (NtrTpost)1/2log⁡(Nco)=o(ζ2)(N_{tr}T_{post})^{1/2}\log(N_{co})=o(\zeta^2)(Ntr​Tpost​)1/2log(Nco​)=o(ζ2), and let Assumptions 1 to 4 hold. Then SDID is asymptotically linear:

τ^sdid−τ=1Ntr∑i=Nco+1N(1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1Tεit−Ei,preψ)+op((NtrTpost)−1/2)(25)\hat{\tau}^{sdid}-\tau=\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}\left(\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}\varepsilon_{it}-\mathbf{E}_{i,pre}\psi\right)+o_p\left(\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{-1/2}\right) \tag{25}τ^sdid−τ=Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​​Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​εit​−Ei,pre​ψ​+op​((Ntr​Tpost​)−1/2)(25)

and consequently asymptotically normal:

(τ^sdid−τ)/Vτ1/2⇒N(0,1),Vτ=1Ntrvar[1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1Tεit−Ei,preψ](26)\left(\hat{\tau}^{sdid}-\tau\right)/V_{\tau}^{1/2}\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}\left(0,1\right),\qquad V_{\tau}=\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\text{var}\left[\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}\varepsilon_{it}-\mathbf{E}_{i,pre}\psi\right] \tag{26}(τ^sdid−τ)/Vτ1/2​⇒N(0,1),Vτ​=Ntr​1​var​Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​εit​−Ei,pre​ψ​(26)

where VτV_{\tau}Vτ​ is of order 1/(NtrTpost)1/(N_{tr}T_{post})1/(Ntr​Tpost​). The variance is the one that would be obtained if L\mathbf{L}L and Σ\SigmaΣ were known: the estimator behaves like the average over treated units of the post-treatment error minus its best linear prediction from that unit's pre-treatment errors. Only the errors of the treated units appear, because the control block is much larger than the treated block. The proof follows the three-term decomposition. Assumption 4 makes the oracle confounding bias negligible. The oracle noise reduces to the leading term because ω~co\tilde{\omega}_{co}ω~co​ is dispersed and λ~pre\tilde{\lambda}_{pre}λ~pre​ is close to ψ\psiψ. The deviation from the oracle is shown to be of smaller order, which uses the lower bound on ζ\zetaζ and the spectral condition on Lco,pre\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}Lco,pre​. The details are in the online appendix.

Large-Sample Inference

Confidence intervals take the form τ∈τ^sdid±zα/2V^τ\tau\in\hat{\tau}^{sdid}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat{V}_{\tau}}τ∈τ^sdid±zα/2​V^τ​​, with three estimators of the variance.

  • Bootstrap (Algorithm 2): for b=1,…,Bb=1,\dots,Bb=1,…,B, draw NNN rows of (Y,W)(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{W})(Y,W) with replacement to form (Y(b),W(b))(\mathbf{Y}^{(b)},\mathbf{W}^{(b)})(Y(b),W(b)), redraw if the sample has no treated or no control units, and compute the SDID estimate τ^(b)\hat{\tau}^{(b)}τ^(b) with re-estimated weights. The variance estimate is the first equation below. Resampling units respects serial correlation within units. The method suits large panels with many treated units, and its drawback is the cost of running the full algorithm in each replication.

  • Jackknife (Algorithm 3): holding ω^\hat{\omega}ω^ and λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^ fixed, for each unit iii re-run the weighted regression without unit iii to obtain τ^(−i)\hat{\tau}^{(-i)}τ^(−i). The variance estimate is the second equation below. SDID is run only once. The jackknife is not defined when Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1.

  • Placebo (Algorithm 4): for b=1,…,Bb=1,\dots,Bb=1,…,B, sample NtrN_{tr}Ntr​ of the NcoN_{co}Nco​ control units without replacement, treat them as if exposed through a placebo assignment matrix Wco,⋅(b)\mathbf{W}^{(b)}_{co,\cdot}Wco,⋅(b)​, and compute the SDID estimate τ^(b)\hat{\tau}^{(b)}τ^(b) on the control data (Yco,⋅,Wco,⋅(b))(\mathbf{Y}_{co,\cdot},\mathbf{W}^{(b)}_{co,\cdot})(Yco,⋅​,Wco,⋅(b)​). The variance estimate V^τplacebo\hat{V}^{placebo}_{\tau}V^τplacebo​ is the variance of these estimates, with the same formula as the bootstrap. It is the only option when Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1. Its validity rests on homoskedasticity across units, because the noise of the treated units is learned from the controls alone.

The bootstrap (and placebo) variance is:

V^τb=1B∑b=1B(τ^(b)−1B∑b=1Bτ^(b))2(27)\hat{V}^{b}_{\tau}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left(\hat{\tau}^{(b)}-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{\tau}^{(b)}\right)^2 \tag{27}V^τb​=B1​b=1∑B​(τ^(b)−B1​b=1∑B​τ^(b))2(27)

and the jackknife variance is:

V^τjack=(N−1)N−1∑i=1N(τ^(−i)−τ^)2(28)\hat{V}^{jack}_{\tau}=\left(N-1\right)N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\hat{\tau}^{(-i)}-\hat{\tau}\right)^2 \tag{28}V^τjack​=(N−1)N−1i=1∑N​(τ^(−i)−τ^)2(28)

Theorem 2 states that if the elements of L\mathbf{L}L are bounded then, under the conditions of Theorem 1, the jackknife is conservative for any 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, and it is exact if treatment effects are constant, τit=τ\tau_{it}=\tauτit​=τ, and the time weights predict well on the treated units:

lim inf⁡Pr⁡[τ∈τ^sdid±zα/2V^τjack]≥1−αTpostNtr−1∥λ^0+Ltr,preλ^pre−Ltr,postλ^post∥22→p0(29)\begin{aligned} \liminf\Pr\left[\tau\in\hat{\tau}^{sdid}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\hat{V}^{jack}_{\tau}}\right]&\geq1-\alpha\\ T_{post}N_{tr}^{-1}\lVert\hat{\lambda}_0+\mathbf{L}_{tr,pre}\hat{\lambda}_{pre}-\mathbf{L}_{tr,post}\hat{\lambda}_{post}\rVert_2^2&\to_p0 \end{aligned} \tag{29}liminfPr[τ∈τ^sdid±zα/2​V^τjack​​]Tpost​Ntr−1​∥λ^0​+Ltr,pre​λ^pre​−Ltr,post​λ^post​∥22​​≥1−α→p​0​(29)

With heterogeneous effects the jackknife implicitly treats the estimand as random, which produces excess estimated variance. The result is specific to SDID. The analogous jackknife for SC would be severely biased upwards, even in the well-specified fixed effects model, and is not recommended.

Coverage of nominal 95 percent intervals in the placebo designs (400 replications) is close to nominal for SDID. In the CPS baseline it is 0.96 with the bootstrap, 0.93 with the jackknife and 0.95 with the placebo method, against 0.89, 0.92 and 0.96 for DID. Coverage is low wherever bias dominates. With the unemployment rate it is 0.78, 0.71 and 0.74 for SDID and 0.38, 0.42 and 0.41 for DID. In the Penn World Table design with education assignment, SDID covers at 0.95, 0.95 and 0.99, and DID at 0.30, 0.34 and 0.94. With Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1 only the placebo method is available, and it covers at 0.97 for SDID.

Related Methods and Staggered Adoption

The augmented SC estimator of Ben-Michael, Feller and Rothstein (2018) combines SC weights with a regression adjustment based on lagged outcomes. With a linear outcome model it is very similar to SDID. It would be equivalent if ω^sdid\hat{\omega}^{sdid}ω^sdid were fitted without intercept and the outcome model were fitted by least squares on the controls with non-negative coefficients that sum to one. Least squares estimators of interactive fixed effects models require a known rank (or a known upper bound) and non-zero singular values of L\mathbf{L}L well separated from zero, and SDID requires neither. Approaches that regress the treated unit on control units typically assume stationarity. The present results take L\mathbf{L}L as deterministic and allow non-stationary errors.

With staggered adoption the weighted regression does not apply directly. The appendix proposes to apply SDID once for every adoption date: form for each date a sample that has the block structure (the never-treated units together with the units adopting at that date, or alternatively a split by time periods), estimate the effect in each sample, and average the estimates with weights equal to each sample's share of treated unit-period pairs.

This is the definition of the SDID estimator: a least squares regression of YitY_{it}Yit​ on an intercept μ\muμ, unit effects αi\alpha_iαi​, time effects βt\beta_tβt​ and the treatment indicator WitW_{it}Wit​, in which cell (i,t)(i,t)(i,t) receives the product weight ω^isdidλ^tsdid\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_i\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}_tω^isdid​λ^tsdid​. The unit weights come from equation (4) and the time weights from equation (7). Treated units all have weight Ntr−1N_{tr}^{-1}Ntr−1​ and post-treatment periods all have weight Tpost−1T_{post}^{-1}Tpost−1​, so the data-dependent part of the weights only concerns the control units and the pre-treatment periods.

The weights make the regression local. A control unit with ω^isdid=0\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_i=0ω^isdid​=0 drops out, and a pre-treatment period with λ^tsdid=0\hat{\lambda}^{sdid}_t=0λ^tsdid​=0 drops out, so the parallel-trends restriction implicit in the additive structure μ+αi+βt\mu+\alpha_i+\beta_tμ+αi​+βt​ only has to hold on the reweighted sample. The parameters μ\muμ, α\alphaα and β\betaβ are not separately identified (a constant can be moved between them), but τ^sdid\hat{\tau}^{sdid}τ^sdid is unique. Because the assignment is a block and the weights are products, the coefficient has a closed form, derived in equation (8):

τ^sdid=1Ntr∑i=Nco+1Nδ^isdid−∑i=1Ncoω^isdidδ^isdid\hat{\tau}^{sdid}=\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}\hat{\delta}^{sdid}_i-\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\hat{\omega}^{sdid}_i\hat{\delta}^{sdid}_iτ^sdid=Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​δ^isdid​−i=1∑Nco​​ω^isdid​δ^isdid​

with δ^isdid\hat{\delta}^{sdid}_iδ^isdid​ given in equation (9). The identifying variation is the change in the treated units' outcomes between the weighted pre-treatment periods and the post-treatment periods, relative to the same change for the weighted control units. Equation (2) is the special case of equal weights and equation (3) drops αi\alpha_iαi​ and the time weights.

This is the standard two-way fixed effects (DID) regression. It is equation (1) with every cell weighted equally. All terms have the same meaning as there: μ\muμ is the intercept, αi\alpha_iαi​ the unit effect, βt\beta_tβt​ the time effect and τ\tauτ the coefficient on WitW_{it}Wit​. Under block assignment the regression is a comparison of four block means. The argument in the derivation of equation (8) applies with all weights equal to one, and after dividing each block by its number of cells it gives

τ^did=(Yˉtr,post−Yˉtr,pre)−(Yˉco,post−Yˉco,pre)\hat{\tau}^{did}=\left(\bar{Y}_{tr,post}-\bar{Y}_{tr,pre}\right)-\left(\bar{Y}_{co,post}-\bar{Y}_{co,pre}\right)τ^did=(Yˉtr,post​−Yˉtr,pre​)−(Yˉco,post​−Yˉco,pre​)

where Yˉg,s\bar{Y}_{g,s}Yˉg,s​ is the unweighted mean of YitY_{it}Yit​ over units in group ggg and periods in block sss. In the notation of equation (8) this is ω^idid=Nco−1\hat{\omega}^{did}_i=N_{co}^{-1}ω^idid​=Nco−1​ together with δ^idid\hat{\delta}^{did}_iδ^idid​ from equation (9).

The estimator is unbiased when the systematic component is additive, Lit=αi+βtL_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_tLit​=αi​+βt​, which is the parallel-trends assumption: every control unit and every pre-treatment period is then an equally valid comparison. What the form rules out is an interactive component in LitL_{it}Lit​ that is correlated with assignment. In the factor model of equation (10) such a component makes DID biased, and it is the reason for the weights in equation (1). DID is the benchmark in the application and in all simulations.

This is the synthetic control estimator written as a weighted regression, so that it can be compared with equations (1) and (2). Relative to equation (1) there are two differences: the unit effects αi\alpha_iαi​ are absent, and there are no time weights (every period has weight one). The unit weights ω^isc\hat{\omega}^{sc}_iω^isc​ are non-negative, sum to one over the control units and equal Ntr−1N_{tr}^{-1}Ntr−1​ for treated units. They come from the problem in equation (4) without the intercept ω0\omega_0ω0​ and with only minimal regularization.

Solving the regression (see the derivation of equation (9)) gives

τ^sc=1Tpost∑t=Tpre+1T(1Ntr∑i=Nco+1NYit−∑i=1Ncoω^iscYit)\hat{\tau}^{sc}=\frac{1}{T_{post}}\sum_{t=T_{pre}+1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}Y_{it}-\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\hat{\omega}^{sc}_iY_{it}\right)τ^sc=Tpost​1​t=Tpre​+1∑T​(Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​Yit​−i=1∑Nco​​ω^isc​Yit​)

which is the familiar SC estimator: the post-treatment gap between the treated average and the synthetic control. The pre-treatment observations enter only through the weights and not through the regression, because the time effects βt\beta_tβt​ fit each pre-treatment period separately.

Without αi\alpha_iαi​ the estimator is not invariant to adding a constant to all outcomes of one unit. A level difference between the treated units and the weighted controls that remains after weighting goes directly into τ^sc\hat{\tau}^{sc}τ^sc. This is why SC needs the weighted controls to match the treated pre-treatment path in levels, while SDID only needs it to be parallel. The time effects βt\beta_tβt​ do make SC invariant to common shocks in each period.

The first line is the objective that determines the unit weights, and the second line is the set of admissible weights. For each pre-treatment period ttt, the term in parentheses is the gap between the weighted average of control outcomes, shifted by the intercept ω0\omega_0ω0​, and the average treated outcome. The first term of ℓunit\ell_{unit}ℓunit​ is the sum of squared gaps over the TpreT_{pre}Tpre​ pre-treatment periods, and the second term is a ridge penalty on the weights with strength ζ2Tpre\zeta^2T_{pre}ζ2Tpre​, where ζ\zetaζ is set in equation (5).

The set Ω\OmegaΩ contains vectors of length NNN. The control entries are non-negative and sum to one, as in the original synthetic control method, so the synthetic control is a convex combination of control units and never extrapolates. The treated entries are fixed at Ntr−1N_{tr}^{-1}Ntr−1​. They only contribute the constant Ntr−1N_{tr}^{-1}Ntr−1​ to ∥ω∥22\lVert\omega\rVert_2^2∥ω∥22​ and do not affect the minimizer.

The intercept ω0\omega_0ω0​ is free. It absorbs any constant level difference, so the weights are chosen to make the weighted control path parallel to the treated path and not equal to it. This is legitimate because equation (1) contains unit effects. Concentrating out ω0\omega_0ω0​ shows that the problem is the SC problem applied to outcomes demeaned over the pre-treatment periods:

min⁡ω0∑t=1Tpre(ω0+gt)2=∑t=1Tpre(gt−1Tpre∑l=1Tpregl)2,gt=∑i=1NcoωiYit−1Ntr∑i=Nco+1NYit\min_{\omega_0}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\left(\omega_0+g_t\right)^2=\sum_{t=1}^{T_{pre}}\left(g_t-\frac{1}{T_{pre}}\sum_{l=1}^{T_{pre}}g_l\right)^2,\qquad g_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{co}}\omega_iY_{it}-\frac{1}{N_{tr}}\sum_{i=N_{co}+1}^{N}Y_{it}ω0​min​t=1∑Tpre​​(ω0​+gt​)2=t=1∑Tpre​​​gt​−Tpre​1​l=1∑Tpre​​gl​​2,gt​=i=1∑Nco​​ωi​Yit​−Ntr​1​i=Nco​+1∑N​Yit​

The ridge penalty pushes the control weights towards the uniform weights Nco−1N_{co}^{-1}Nco−1​, which minimize ∥ω∥22\lVert\omega\rVert_2^2∥ω∥22​ on the simplex. It makes the solution unique and less sparse, and it limits the variance contribution of the control units, which is proportional to ∥ωco∥22\lVert\omega_{co}\rVert_2^2∥ωco​∥22​ (see equation (19)). The expected value of this objective is computed in equation (17).

This sets the regularization parameter of the unit-weight problem in equation (4). The quantity σ^2\hat{\sigma}^2σ^2 is the sample variance of the first differences Δit\Delta_{it}Δit​ defined in equation (6), computed over control units and pre-treatment periods. It measures the size of a typical one-period change of the outcome and so has the units of the outcome. First differences are used so that persistent level differences between units do not inflate the scale.

Because the fit term in equation (4) is a sum of TpreT_{pre}Tpre​ squared gaps measured in outcome units, the penalty ζ2Tpre∥ω∥22\zeta^2T_{pre}\lVert\omega\rVert_2^2ζ2Tpre​∥ω∥22​ with ζ\zetaζ proportional to σ^\hat{\sigma}σ^ is on the same scale, and the weights are invariant to rescaling the outcome.

The factor (NtrTpost)1/4\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{1/4}(Ntr​Tpost​)1/4 comes from the theory. Theorem 1 (equation (25)) requires

(NtrTpost)1/2log⁡(Nco)=o(ζ2)\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{1/2}\log\left(N_{co}\right)=o\left(\zeta^2\right)(Ntr​Tpost​)1/2log(Nco​)=o(ζ2)

and the choice here gives ζ2=(NtrTpost)1/2σ^2\zeta^2=\left(N_{tr}T_{post}\right)^{1/2}\hat{\sigma}^2ζ2=(Ntr​Tpost​)1/2σ^2, which matches this rate up to the logarithmic factor. The larger the treated block, the more precise the estimator of τ\tauτ can be, and the more the weights must be dispersed so that the noise carried by the control units stays below that level. In the California application NtrTpost=12N_{tr}T_{post}=12Ntr​Tpost​=12, so ζ=121/4σ^≈1.86σ^\zeta=12^{1/4}\hat{\sigma}\approx1.86\hat{\sigma}ζ=121/4σ^≈1.86σ^. For the time weights the implementation uses the negligible value ζ=10−6σ^\zeta=10^{-6}\hat{\sigma}ζ=10−6σ^, only to select a unique minimizer.

These are the two ingredients of σ^2\hat{\sigma}^2σ^2 in equation (5). The first difference Δit\Delta_{it}Δit​ is the change in the outcome of unit iii from period ttt to period t+1t+1t+1. It is used only for control units, i=1,…,Ncoi=1,\dots,N_{co}i=1,…,Nco​, and for t=1,…,Tpre−1t=1,\dots,T_{pre}-1t=1,…,Tpre​−1, so that both periods of every difference lie before treatment. There are Nco(Tpre−1)N_{co}\left(T_{pre}-1\right)Nco​(Tpre​−1) such differences, and Δˉ\bar{\Delta}Δˉ is their mean, the average one-period change (the common drift) of the control outcomes before treatment.

Subtracting Δˉ\bar{\Delta}Δˉ in equation (5) removes that common drift, so σ^\hat{\sigma}σ^ measures the dispersion of one-period changes around it. Differencing removes any unit fixed effect, since αi\alpha_iαi​ cancels in Yi(t+1)−YitY_{i(t+1)}-Y_{it}Yi(t+1)​−Yit​. If the outcome were Yit=αi+βt+εitY_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_t+\varepsilon_{it}Yit​=αi​+βt​+εit​ with independent errors of variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 and a linear time effect, then

Δit−Δˉ≈εi(t+1)−εit,E[σ^2]≈2σ2\Delta_{it}-\bar{\Delta}\approx\varepsilon_{i(t+1)}-\varepsilon_{it},\qquad E\left[\hat{\sigma}^2\right]\approx2\sigma^2Δit​−Δˉ≈εi(t+1)​−εit​,E[σ^2]≈2σ2

so σ^\hat{\sigma}σ^ is a noise scale of the same order as σ\sigmaσ. In the California application there are 38×18=68438\times18=68438×18=684 differences.

This is the mirror image of equation (4), with the roles of units and periods exchanged. For each control unit iii, the term in parentheses is the gap between a weighted average of its pre-treatment outcomes, shifted by the intercept λ0\lambda_0λ0​, and its average post-treatment outcome. The objective sums the squared gaps over the NcoN_{co}Nco​ control units. Only control units are used, because for them the post-treatment outcomes are not affected by treatment.

The set Λ\LambdaΛ contains vectors of length TTT: the pre-treatment entries are non-negative and sum to one, and the post-treatment entries are fixed at Tpost−1T_{post}^{-1}Tpost−1​. The weights therefore pick a convex combination of pre-treatment periods that predicts, for the control units, the post-treatment average up to a constant. The intercept λ0\lambda_0λ0​ absorbs a common shift between the two sets of periods. It plays the role of the time effects in equation (1), just as ω0\omega_0ω0​ in equation (4) is justified by the unit effects.

The weights enter the estimator through δ^isdid\hat{\delta}^{sdid}_iδ^isdid​ in equation (9). If outcomes drift, periods far in the past predict the post-treatment level poorly and receive little weight, which is why the weights in the application concentrate on the years just before 1989.

There is no ridge penalty. In the model the errors of a unit are correlated over time, and this correlation is useful for prediction, so the weights should be free to exploit it. The expected objective in equation (18) already contains a penalty generated by the noise, which shrinks the weights towards the vector ψ\psiψ of equation (21).

This is the data-generating model behind the simulations, in matrix form. Y\mathbf{Y}Y, L\mathbf{L}L, W\mathbf{W}W and E\mathbf{E}E are N×TN\times TN×T matrices with elements YitY_{it}Yit​, LitL_{it}Lit​, WitW_{it}Wit​ and εit\varepsilon_{it}εit​, and τ\tauτ is a constant treatment effect (set to zero in the placebo studies). The systematic component is Lit=γiυt⊤L_{it}=\gamma_i\upsilon_t^{\top}Lit​=γi​υt⊤​: unit iii has a vector of RRR latent characteristics γi\gamma_iγi​ (a row of Γ\mathbf{\Gamma}Γ), period ttt has a vector of RRR latent shocks υt\upsilon_tυt​ (a row of Υ\mathbf{\Upsilon}Υ), and each unit responds to the common shocks with its own loadings. L\mathbf{L}L has rank at most RRR.

The two-way fixed effects model is the special case with R=2R=2R=2:

γi=(αi,1),υt=(1,βt),Lit=γiυt⊤=αi+βt\gamma_i=\left(\alpha_i,1\right),\qquad\upsilon_t=\left(1,\beta_t\right),\qquad L_{it}=\gamma_i\upsilon_t^{\top}=\alpha_i+\beta_tγi​=(αi​,1),υt​=(1,βt​),Lit​=γi​υt⊤​=αi​+βt​

so the factor model nests DID and adds interactions such as γi3υt3\gamma_{i3}\upsilon_{t3}γi3​υt3​, under which units have different trends. If such loadings differ between treated and control units, parallel trends fails.

The model separates two things. Assignment W\mathbf{W}W may depend on L\mathbf{L}L, which is selection on persistent unobservables, and this is the source of bias. Assignment may not depend on E\mathbf{E}E, which has conditional mean zero. The methods compared differ in how they remove L\mathbf{L}L: DID differences out an additive L\mathbf{L}L, SC balances Γ\mathbf{\Gamma}Γ with unit weights, SDID does both and also balances Υ\mathbf{\Upsilon}Υ with time weights, and the matrix completion estimator estimates L\mathbf{L}L directly. Equation (11) splits L\mathbf{L}L into its additive and interactive parts, and equation (13) generalizes the model to heterogeneous effects.

The additive part F\mathbf{F}F is the least squares projection of L\mathbf{L}L on the set of matrices of the form ai+bta_i+b_tai​+bt​. Start from

ai+bˉ=1T∑l=1TLil,aˉ+bt=1N∑j=1NLjta_i+\bar{b}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{l=1}^{T}L_{il},\qquad\bar{a}+b_t=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}L_{jt}ai​+bˉ=T1​l=1∑T​Lil​,aˉ+bt​=N1​j=1∑N​Ljt​

F\mathbf{F}F is the part of the signal that DID removes exactly, and M\mathbf{M}M is the part that can bias it.

This is the assignment mechanism of the placebo simulations. Each unit is exposed (Di=1D_i=1Di​=1) with probability πi\pi_iπi​, independently across units, and exposed units are treated in the periods after T0T_0T0​. The probability is a logistic function of the unit's additive effect αi\alpha_iαi​ and of its row Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​ of the interactive component from equation (11), with coefficients ϕα\phi_{\alpha}ϕα​ (a scalar) and ϕM\phi_MϕM​ (a vector conformable with Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​). Since M\mathbf{M}M has low rank, Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​ lies in a low-dimensional space.

Two features matter. First, the conditioning set contains Ei\mathbf{E}_iEi​, but πi\pi_iπi​ does not depend on it. Assignment is therefore independent of the errors, which is the exogeneity condition of equation (10), and no method is biased because of E\mathbf{E}E. Second, πi\pi_iπi​ depends on Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​, so treated and control units differ systematically in the interactive component and their trends are not parallel. The implied log odds are linear:

log⁡πi1−πi=ϕααi+ϕMMi\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\phi_{\alpha}\alpha_i+\phi_M\mathbf{M}_ilog1−πi​πi​​=ϕα​αi​+ϕM​Mi​

Dependence on αi\alpha_iαi​ alone would be harmless for DID and SDID, which remove unit effects, but not for SC. Dependence on Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​ is what biases DID. With ϕα=0\phi_{\alpha}=0ϕα​=0 and ϕM=0\phi_M=0ϕM​=0 the probability is 1/21/21/2 for every unit, assignment is completely random, and all estimators are unbiased.

The coefficients are not chosen freely. They are fitted by logistic regression of real state policies on αi\alpha_iαi​ and Mi\mathbf{M}_iMi​, so the strength of selection in the simulation is as realistic as the outcome model.

The paper prints this as one display with the two groups of terms labelled bias and noise, and the note names them BBB and ε\varepsilonε; the content is identical. For deterministic weights B(ω,λ)B(\omega,\lambda)B(ω,λ) is non-random, because L\mathbf{L}L is fixed, and ε(ω,λ)\varepsilon(\omega,\lambda)ε(ω,λ) has mean zero, so BBB is the bias of τ^(ω,λ)\hat{\tau}(\omega,\lambda)τ^(ω,λ). For the data-dependent weights ω^\hat{\omega}ω^ and λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^ the identity still holds, but the two terms are no longer a bias and a mean-zero noise, which is why oracle weights are introduced in equation (16). In the two-way model Lit=αi+βtL_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_tLit​=αi​+βt​ the term B(ω,λ)B(\omega,\lambda)B(ω,λ) is zero for all admissible weights, as computed under equation (24).

The oracle weights are the population counterparts of the estimated weights. The estimated weights minimize the random objectives ℓunit\ell_{unit}ℓunit​ of equation (4) and ℓtime\ell_{time}ℓtime​ of equation (7). The oracle weights minimize the expectations of the same objectives over the same sets Ω\OmegaΩ and Λ\LambdaΛ, where the expectation is over the error matrix E\mathbf{E}E with L\mathbf{L}L and W\mathbf{W}W held fixed.

The reason for introducing them is technical but central. The estimator τ^sdid=τ^(ω^,λ^)\hat{\tau}^{sdid}=\hat{\tau}(\hat{\omega},\hat{\lambda})τ^sdid=τ^(ω^,λ^) multiplies the data by weights that were themselves computed from the data, so the bias and noise terms of equation (15) are not separable. The oracle weights ω~\tilde{\omega}ω~ and λ~\tilde{\lambda}λ~ are deterministic. For them B(ω~,λ~)B(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda})B(ω~,λ~) is a number and ε(ω~,λ~)\varepsilon(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda})ε(ω~,λ~) is a linear function of Gaussian errors, so the oracle estimator τ^(ω~,λ~)\hat{\tau}(\tilde{\omega},\tilde{\lambda})τ^(ω~,λ~) is easy to analyze. The proof strategy, laid out in equation (19), is to show that the feasible estimator is close to the oracle estimator.

The oracle weights are infeasible, since they depend on the unknown L\mathbf{L}L and Σ\SigmaΣ, and they are used only in the analysis. Equations (17) and (18) evaluate the two expectations in closed form. The assumptions in equations (23) and (24) are stated for the oracle weights, which makes them conditions on L\mathbf{L}L, Σ\SigmaΣ and the design and not on the realized data.

ψ=Σpre,pre−1Σpre,postλpost\psi=\Sigma_{pre,pre}^{-1}\Sigma_{pre,post}\lambda_{post}ψ=Σpre,pre−1​Σpre,post​λpost​

The regression interpretation is direct. For one unit, Σpre,pre\Sigma_{pre,pre}Σpre,pre​ is the variance of its pre-treatment errors and Σpre,postλpost\Sigma_{pre,post}\lambda_{post}Σpre,post​λpost​ is their covariance with the average post-treatment error Ei,postλpost\mathbf{E}_{i,post}\lambda_{post}Ei,post​λpost​, so ψ\psiψ is the population least squares coefficient of the latter on the former. If Σ\SigmaΣ is diagonal, Σpre,post=0\Sigma_{pre,post}=0Σpre,post​=0 and ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0.

One caveat on the middle expression of the target. Read literally as the Euclidean norm of the vector Σ~(v⊤,λpost⊤)⊤\tilde{\Sigma}(v^{\top},\lambda_{post}^{\top})^{\top}Σ~(v⊤,λpost⊤​)⊤, its minimizer is in general not ψ\psiψ, because that vector also contains the block −Σpost,prev+Σpost,postλpost-\Sigma_{post,pre}v+\Sigma_{post,post}\lambda_{post}−Σpost,pre​v+Σpost,post​λpost​. The stated solution is the minimizer of the quadratic form above, that is, of the norm with Σ~1/2\tilde{\Sigma}^{1/2}Σ~1/2 in place of Σ~\tilde{\Sigma}Σ~. This is the same imprecision as in equation (18).

This is the condition of Assumption 3 on the systematic component. σR(Lco,pre)\sigma_R(\mathbf{L}_{co,pre})σR​(Lco,pre​) is the RRR-th largest singular value of the control, pre-treatment block of L\mathbf{L}L, and RRR is the largest integer below min⁡(Tpre,Nco)\sqrt{\min(T_{pre},N_{co})}min(Tpre​,Nco​)​. The condition says that this singular value, divided by RRR, is of smaller order than both Ntr−1/2log⁡−1/2(Nco)N_{tr}^{-1/2}\log^{-1/2}(N_{co})Ntr−1/2​log−1/2(Nco​) and Tpost−1/2log⁡−1/2(Tpre)T_{post}^{-1/2}\log^{-1/2}(T_{pre})Tpost−1/2​log−1/2(Tpre​).

In words, Lco,pre\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}Lco,pre​ may have at most about min⁡(Tpre,Nco)\sqrt{\min(T_{pre},N_{co})}min(Tpre​,Nco​)​ singular values that matter; beyond that index they must be very small. The condition is an approximate low-rank requirement. If the rank of Lco,pre\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}Lco,pre​ is below RRR, then σR(Lco,pre)=0\sigma_R(\mathbf{L}_{co,pre})=0σR​(Lco,pre​)=0 and the condition holds trivially. In the two-way model Lit=αi+βtL_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_tLit​=αi​+βt​ the rank is at most two.

Two things are not required. The rank need not be known or estimated. There is also no lower bound on the non-zero singular values, so weak factors are allowed, which is the main difference from least squares estimation of interactive fixed effects, where the factors must be strong enough to be recovered.

The condition is used to control the third term of equation (19), the deviation from the oracle. The estimated weights are fitted on the noisy block Yco,pre\mathbf{Y}_{co,pre}Yco,pre​. If Lco,pre\mathbf{L}_{co,pre}Lco,pre​ had many large singular values, the weights could fit many directions of the signal, their effective number of free parameters would be large, and the estimated weights would not concentrate around the oracle weights. The thresholds scale with Ntr−1/2N_{tr}^{-1/2}Ntr−1/2​ and Tpost−1/2T_{post}^{-1/2}Tpost−1/2​ because the target precision is (NtrTpost)−1/2(N_{tr}T_{post})^{-1/2}(Ntr​Tpost​)−1/2: a larger treated block demands a tighter approximation.

These are the first four conditions of Assumption 4, two for the oracle unit weights and two for the oracle time weights of equations (17) and (18). In each pair, one condition says that the weights are dispersed and the other says that they fit on their training block.

Line 1 bounds the norm of the control weights. Uniform weights have ∥ω~co∥2=Nco−1/2\lVert\tilde{\omega}_{co}\rVert_2=N_{co}^{-1/2}∥ω~co​∥2​=Nco−1/2​, the smallest possible value, and the condition then reads NtrTpostlog⁡(Nco)/Nco→0N_{tr}T_{post}\log(N_{co})/N_{co}\to0Ntr​Tpost​log(Nco​)/Nco​→0. It ensures that the noise carried by the control units is negligible relative to the target precision (NtrTpost)−1/2(N_{tr}T_{post})^{-1/2}(Ntr​Tpost​)−1/2.

Line 2 bounds the pre-treatment fit error of the oracle row regression, the vector that also appears in equation (17). Here the paper prints max⁡(Nco,Tpost)\max(N_{co},T_{post})max(Nco​,Tpost​), and the note reproduces it, while Assumption 2(iii) contains max⁡(Ntr,Tpost)\max(N_{tr},T_{post})max(Ntr​,Tpost​). This is the identifying assumption of the paper. The conditions in equation (23) concern what the weights do on the blocks where they are fitted (control units, pre-treatment periods) and could in principle be assessed. It states that the treated block is not exceptional in a way that the weights cannot reproduce, and it has the same status as parallel trends for DID. By equation (20) it holds if either the unit weights or the time weights generalize to the treated block, or if their errors offset.

This is the variance estimator of the bootstrap (Algorithm 2), and the same formula is used for the placebo method (Algorithm 4). τ^(b)\hat{\tau}^{(b)}τ^(b) is the SDID estimate computed on the bbb-th artificial dataset, BBB is the number of replications, and the inner average is the mean of the BBB estimates. What differs between the two methods is how the artificial datasets are produced. In the bootstrap, whole units (rows of Y\mathbf{Y}Y and W\mathbf{W}W) are drawn with replacement, which keeps the time-series dependence of each unit intact, and the weights are estimated again in each draw, so the uncertainty from estimating the weights is included. The spread of τ^(b)\hat{\tau}^{(b)}τ^(b) then mimics the sampling variation of τ^sdid\hat{\tau}^{sdid}τ^sdid across units, which by equation (25) is driven by the treated units. This needs several treated units; with Ntr=1N_{tr}=1Ntr​=1 every valid draw contains the same treated unit and its noise is not captured.

In the placebo method only control units are used. NtrN_{tr}Ntr​ of them are labelled as treated although their true effect is zero, so τ^(b)\hat{\tau}^{(b)}τ^(b) is pure estimation error and its variance estimates VτV_{\tau}Vτ​ of equation (26) directly. This is valid only if the errors of the control units have the same distribution as those of the treated units (homoskedasticity across units), since the treated units' own noise is never used.

The formula is the standard delete-one jackknife applied to the weighted regression of equation (1), with ω^\hat{\omega}ω^ and λ^\hat{\lambda}λ^ held fixed: τ^(−i)\hat{\tau}^{(-i)}τ^(−i) is the coefficient when unit iii is removed, and τ^\hat{\tau}τ^ is the full-sample estimate. With unit iii removed, the regression still has product weights and block assignment, so by the last remark in the derivation of equation (8) its coefficient is the double difference with the weights normalized again within each group. The time weights are unchanged, so the adjusted outcomes δ^j\hat{\delta}_jδ^j​ of equation (9) are unchanged. The condition says that time weights fitted on the control units also predict well for the treated units, the second half of the column-regression condition discussed under equation (20). For SC there are no time weights and no unit effects to remove this variation, which is why the analogous jackknife is badly biased upwards.
